questions.question: What are symbols in Ruby?
questions.title: Symbols in Ruby
questions.direct_answer: A symbol is an immutable, interned identifier: :name. The same symbol is always the same object (object_id matches), so they're memory-efficient and compare by identity. Strings are mutable text (new object each time); symbols are fixed identifiers (one copy forever). Use symbols for hash keys, method names, config keys — anything that's an identifier, not data. You can't concatenate (:a + :b raises) or change them, but :a.to_s gives 'a' and 'a'.to_sym gives :a. In modern Ruby (1.9+), hash literals use symbols: {name: 'Ada'} is { :name => 'Ada' }. Symbols as hash keys are faster to compare than strings and don't create a new object on each lookup. Rule: symbols for identifiers/keys, strings for text you display or change.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know a symbol is an immutable interned identifier (same object every time) used for keys/identifiers.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using strings for hash keys (a new object each time — use symbols), or treating symbols as strings (:a + :b raises).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Symbols = immutable interned identifiers (:name; same object every time). Use for keys/identifiers. Convert with to_s/to_sym. Can't concatenate.

sections.title: Immutable Identifiers
sections.content: A symbol is an immutable, interned identifier: name. The same symbol is always the same object (object_id matches), so they're memory-efficient and compare by identity. Strings are mutable text (new object each time); symbols are fixed identifiers (one copy forever). Use symbols for hash keys, method names, config keys — anything that's an identifier, not data. You can't concatenate (a symbol plus b symbol raises) or change them, but a symbol to_s gives a string and a string to_sym gives a symbol. In modern Ruby (1.9 plus), hash literals use symbols: name Ada is name arrow Ada. Symbols as hash keys are faster to compare than strings and don't create a new object on each lookup. Rule: symbols for identifiers and keys, strings for text you display or change.

sections.title: Symbols
sections.content:
immutable interned identifiers; same object every time. Keys/identifiers. to_s/to_sym.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Sy[:name] --> I[interned: same object_id]
  Sy --> M[immutable: can't change]
  Sy --> U[use for keys/identifiers]
  C[convert] --> S[:a.to_s -> 'a']
  C --> R['a'.to_sym -> :a]
```

sections.title: Symbols
sections.content:
```ruby
# A symbol: immutable, interned identifier
:name

# Same symbol = SAME object (interned):
:name.object_id == :name.object_id   # true
# (a new 'name' string each time = DIFFERENT objects)
'name'.object_id == 'name'.object_id   # false

# Symbols are IMMUTABLE (can't change):
# :a + :b            # raises NoMethodError (can't concatenate)
# :a.upcase          # raises (not a string method)

# Convert:
:hello.to_s          # 'hello'   (symbol -> string)
'hello'.to_sym       # :hello    (string -> symbol)

# Use as HASH KEYS (efficient; no new object per lookup):
h = { name: 'Ada', age: 30 }   # { :name => 'Ada', :age => 30 }
h[:name]                       # 'Ada'

# Symbol vs string keys are DIFFERENT keys:
h2 = { 'name' => 'Ada' }
h2[:name]                     # nil  (:name != 'name')

# Use symbols for: hash keys, method names, config keys, states.
# Use strings for: text you display, interpolate, or change.
# Modern Ruby: symbols are GC'd if no longer referenced (since 2.2).
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using strings for hash keys — a new object each time (use symbols).
Treating symbols as strings (:a + :b raises — convert with to_s).
Mixing :name and 'name' as keys — different keys (lookup returns nil).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A symbol is an immutable, interned identifier (:name; same object every time).
Symbols are memory-efficient and compare by identity — use for keys/identifiers.
Strings are mutable text (new object each time); symbols are fixed (one copy).
